# cr-1 -- VRRP for the services subnet's floating gateway.
#
# One instance, on the services interface. The management side
# carries no virtual address: the pair is highly available for traffic
# LEAVING the services subnet, which is what a default gateway is for.
# Traffic entering from management names cr-1 or cr-2 directly.
#
# No authentication block. VRRPv2's shared password is not a security
# control -- RFC 5798 dropped it precisely because it authenticates
# nothing against an attacker who can already inject on the segment --
# and this segment is a private bridge with no host address on it.
# Writing one here would look like a control without being one.
#
# preempt is left at its default (on): cr-1 is the designated master by
# priority and takes the address back when it returns, so steady state
# is always the same router, which is the state anything debugging this
# will assume.
global_defs {
    router_id cr-1
}

vrrp_instance services_gw {
    state MASTER
    interface services
    virtual_router_id 150
    priority 200
    advert_int 1
    virtual_ipaddress {
        192.168.150.254/24 dev services
    }
}

#
# access_gw -- the same arrangement for the access subnet (#30).
#
# The wireless segment needs a default gateway that survives losing one
# router, exactly as the services subnet does, so this is a second
# instance of the same pattern rather than a new idea. Wireless clients
# are addressed by DHCP and handed 192.168.151.254 as their router;
# whichever of the pair holds it answers.
#
# A DIFFERENT virtual_router_id (151, not 150). VRIDs are scoped per
# segment, so reusing 150 would technically work -- but the two
# instances would be indistinguishable in a packet capture, and if the
# two subnets ever shared a broadcast domain by accident the pair would
# fight over one address. A VRID per subnet costs nothing and makes the
# capture readable.
#
# Same priorities as services_gw, deliberately: cr-1 is master for both,
# so the steady state is one router holding both gateways, and a
# failover moves both together. Splitting them would mean traffic
# between the two subnets crossing the pair mid-path for no benefit.
#
vrrp_instance access_gw {
    state MASTER
    interface access
    virtual_router_id 151
    priority 200
    advert_int 1
    virtual_ipaddress {
        192.168.151.254/24 dev access
    }
}
